James Ketchell - round the world

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
British adventurer James Ketchell sails into Cape Town after months at sea — but this time, it’s not just about breaking records. He’s helping the South African Weather Service drop high-tech se

Unique Selling Point:
An adventurer’s journey meets local science — James Ketchell’s Cape Town landing links exploration with the South African Weather Service’s work to better understand our oceans.

Overview:
British adventurer James Ketchell set sail from Gosport, England, on a nine-month, 30 000-nautical-mile journey around the world.
His goal is to become the first person in history to circle the globe by air, land, and sea.
Along the way, he connects with classrooms across the world — sharing lessons from the ocean and stories of endurance and discovery.

Why Cape Town & South Africa Matter:
Cape Town is one of the key stops on James’s global route. After months alone at sea, he’ll finally reunite with his family for a few days before continuing his voyage.
While here, he’ll also work with the South African Weather Service to drop Argo floats — ocean sensors that gather important information about sea temperatures and currents. This data helps improve weather forecasts and climate research.

What We’ll Cover:
• The journey: James’s world challenge and what drives him to keep going.
• The South African link: Cape Town as a crucial stop where science meets adventure.
• The Argo floats: How they work and how they help local weather scientists.
• The human story: Life alone on the ocean, and the emotional moment of seeing his family again.
• The presenter’s experience: Our presenter will join James on the boat to get a real sense of what it takes to sail one of these yachts — from handling the ropes to facing the wind and waves.
• Visuals: The Cape Town coastline, James’s arrival, his family reunion, the Argo floats, and sailing scenes with the presenter.

Summary:
British adventurer James Ketchell arrives in Cape Town after months at sea on his solo circumnavigation. As part of his mission, he’s partnering with the South African Weather Service to deploy Argo floats — ocean sensors that collect vital climate and marine data. It’s a story that brings together human endurance, ocean science, and South Africa’s role in global research.

Further information:
After months alone at sea, British adventurer James Ketchell is finally making landfall in Cape Town — greeted by his family for the first time in weeks. It’s an emotional reunion marking a rare pause in his nine-month, 30 000-nautical-mile solo voyage around the world.

James is no stranger to pushing limits. He’s rowed across the Atlantic, climbed Mount Everest, and flown a gyrocopter around the globe. Now, his latest challenge brings him to South Africa — not only to continue his record-breaking journey, but also to work with the South African Weather Service. Together, they’ll deploy Argo floats, ocean instruments that drift beneath the waves to collect vital data about our climate and weather.

Through this story, Carte Blanche goes beyond the adventure — exploring the man behind the mission, his long days alone on the ocean, and the brief, heartfelt moments that make the journey worthwhile.

Script:


James: My name is James Ketchell and I'm an adventurer.
Erin: Some people need to know what lies beyond the edge.

James: Driven by something I can't quite name, something that keeps me moving.

Erin: For them, the finish line is just another starting point.
What drives people to risk everything?
James: I keep chasing it across oceans, through storms, through silence.
Erin: That search has led him here...
Subtitles Dealtry Welcome to Cape Town, James!
Upsound Erin After months at sea, James Ketchell has sailed into Cape Town in the latest milestone on his journey around the world. We're at the V&A waterfront to meet the man behind the mission and find out what exactly sets him apart from others who've done the same.
Erin: In July last year, James set sail from Gosport in the UK, to circumnavigate the globe by sea. (Alt take)
Upsound Erin Very well, how are you? Good to see you. Hi James.
Erin: After more than 8,000 nautical miles, James is nowhere near finished.
Upsound James The boat's a bit of a mess at the moment because it's a working boat.
Upsound Erin That's all right.
Upsound Erin: So we start with the easy stuff. Yeah. So for people who have never met you or who are meeting you for the first time, who is James Ketchell? James Ketchell.
Upsound James I am a 43-year-old British guy on my way around the world to see if I can complete my third circumnavigation. And on the way around the world, I want to try and inspire some kids to pursue their own goals and dreams. So that could be a good starting point.
Erin: Not one to brag, James's achievements speak for themselves. Over the past 15 years, he's pushed himself across the planet, surviving setbacks, close calls, and moments that could easily have ended it all.
Upsound: …It was a near-death experience for a British adventurer who was rescued by cargo ship…
Erin: Of all his adventures, three stand above the rest.
Erin: In 2010, he rowed across the Atlantic. In 2011, he summited Everest. And in 2013, he cycled around the world.
Erin: What the media dubbed the ultimate triathlon.
Upsound James The best thing that ever happened to me was I had quite a serious motorbike accident. And the doctor said to me, I don't know if you're going to ever be able to walk again. It really kind of opened your mind up to actually you don't realise what you have until you do not have it anymore. And it gave me a kick up the backside that I think I probably needed. And it was off the back of that that I decided I was going to row a boat across the Atlantic Ocean.
Upsound James And then in 2019, I flew a small gyro plane around the world. Set a Guinness World Record actually. And it was an incredible journey. I've been around the world in the air and on land. How could I come this far and not go around the world on water? And at that point, I made a decision and said, I'm going to sail around the world.
Erin: As the boat undergoes essential repairs, James opens it up to a group of local kids – part of his mission to inspire.
Upsound James I get from one side of Australia to the other.
Erin: They all had the same question: How much does it cost?
Upsound James So this is 2.5 million rand. 2.5 million. I didn't have that money. So I had to find a way to get that money.
And I had to write to thousands of companies to try and get that money. But if you really want it enough, you will find a way to get the money.
Upsound Erin Most people might look at a guy with a yacht and think rich white bloke must be easy for him. Yeah.
Upsound James I wish I was some multi-millionaire crypto trader, but I'm not. But it's really quite the opposite. I'm absolutely broke as I sit here and talk to you completely. That's why people don't do this. Because it's difficult to get to the start line. And it's supposed to be difficult. Otherwise it wouldn't mean anything. I've had to go out and find sponsors, but we're doing it we're here in Cape Town and day by day we're trying to make it happen.
Upsound John Ketchell If he can complete this and become the only human to circumnavigate the globe by air, sea and land, that's quite an achievement because nobody's done it.
Erin: One of the people helping to make this journey easier, is his dad, John Ketchell, who's flown out to visit.
Upsound Erin What's it like being the father of a...
Upsound John Ketchell Crazy man?
Upsound Erin Your words, not mine.
Upsound John Ketchell Well, of course I'm proud. I can't tell him that though. Hopefully when he's done this one, maybe he'll do more simple ones. I've been helping James for the last two years, prepare this boat for his circumnavigation. The only trouble is I'm getting a bit old for going in and out. This is not a nice boat.
Upsound John Ketchell It kills my back the day working on this. But yeah, it's good. Keeps you going.
Erin: John wasn’t lying — this cabin is tiny.
Upsound James Can you see how it just molds around your body? Yeah, it's like a little human glove. You're totally cool. Everyone who comes into the boat has to write a good luck message.
Erin: And yes… I signed it too.
Upsound Erin Thank you, Chef. Adventure food.
Upsound James Good temperature.
Upsound Erin Mmm. It's okay. It's like smash with some veggies in it. It is. It's been a long shoot, though. Ha ha ha.
Upsound James There's an amazing science aspect to the project. I'm an ambassador for the National Oceanography Centre. We're deploying an Argo float in the Indian Ocean. That is super cool. They trust me and they've given me the responsibility to deploy it.
Erin: On his next leg toward Australia, James will carry an Argo float, a sea robot he'll drop into the ocean to collect vital measurements.
Upsound James Someone sent me instructions.
Erin: Once deployed, it joins thousands of other Argo floats worldwide, drifting for years with ocean currents and sending data back to scientists.

Erin: James is heading into the southern Indian Ocean, remote and hard to reach. It plays a crucial role in shaping our weather. That makes him ideal to drop it off.
Upsound Dr Tammy Morris: We've had a few that we've deployed into the retroflexion, the Agulhas Retroflection….
Erin: Working with James on this mission is Dr Tammy Morris. She is the Ocean and Polar Coordinator at the South African Environmental Observation Network.
Upsound Dr Tammy Morris These data have been used just to understand the value and the health of the ocean, basically, and how it's been warming. And this stuff is going into all of our numerical forecast systems. It's going into our daily lives. That information is helping us live a better life. In South Africa we've only managed to buy a few.
Upsound Erin How much are they?
Upsound Dr Tammy Morris They cost about a half a million rand each. As soon as you start adding those extra sensors on, you're getting to two and a half million rand.
Hats off to James going into those oceans on such a small yacht. I would be very nervous myself.
Erin: Dr Morris's concern is understandable. The Southern Ocean is among the most dangerous on Earth.
Erin: James has never sailed it before. So for this leg, he's joined by someone who has – Cape Town yachtsman, Dealtry Pickford.
Upsound Dealtry Pickford James is an amazing adventurer. He's done stuff that most people would never even dream of doing.
Even though you're only two on the boat, you're usually sailing the boat by yourself because the other person is resting. And he needs to rely on me to sail the boat as do I need to rely on him to keep us safe.
Erin: Before they set sail, the yacht must be pushed to its limits. And today, they've allowed me on board.
Upsound Erin It's much nicer being on the boat than in the mall. I must be honest.
Erin: But it turns out to be anything but a leisurely cruise!
Upsound James We have to put the sail up. Erin.
Upsound Erin It's tighter now.
Upsound James Yeah, it's fun, huh?
Upsound Erin It's great. It's a real thrill, I'll tell you.
Upsound James Ketchell It's going to get more challenging where we're going.
Upsound James Ketchell Hold it. Ready? 3, 2, 1.
Upsound Erin Sh*t! Okay.
Upsound Erin There's so much work to be done, constantly calibrating with the wind and the swell. It's a really full-on, hands-on job.
Erin: After a few hours of hauling ropes and battling the wind, I've got a whole new respect for what James does. Back on dry land, there's one last thing to do before they depart.
Upsound Erin Scores of South African children have signed the Argo float, and now it's time for me to make my mark.
Upsound Erin Okay.
Erin: Our name goes onto the float, alongside all the others.
Cargo loaded, crew ready, we wave them off.
Upsound: Good luck guys!
Erin: After weeks of tough sailing, they reach the precise spot to deploy it.
Upsound James We're good. I'm going to rest it up here.
Upsound James Yeah. 3, 2, 1, go!
Upsound James Yes! That's working perfectly.
Upsound James Alright, we've got GPS coordinates as well. Nice work. Look at that!
Erin: Dropping the Argo float is one milestone, but James still has months of tough sailing ahead as he continues his quest to do what no person has done before.









PROMO 1
Erin: An adventurer chasing a world first dream pulls into Cape Town.
UPSOUND – James Ketchell (01:17:59:26 – 01:18:10:39)
Cape Town stop is definitely not a holiday, there's a lot of work to do. Because we're going into the Southern Ocean now.
Erin: He's still only part way through a journey that could make history.
UPSOUND – James Ketchell (01:21:38:23 – 01:22:02:12)
“Right now, this project is my whole purpose… and fingers crossed, I can do it.”

PROMO 2
Erin: An adventurer stops over in Cape Town mid journey around the world.
UPSOUND – James Ketchell (01:15:53:35 – 01:16:02:10)
“I have to make an effort… it’s added to the purpose of going around the world.”
VO – Erin: James Ketchel is chasing a record and in the process helping science too.
UPSOUND – Dr Tammy Morris
We really need to understand how our ocean is working.

PROMO 3
Erin: An adventurer takes on his next big ocean leg, chasing a record and taking on waters that don't forgive mistakes.
UPSOUND – James Ketchell (01:05:05:28 – 01:05:20:12)
“It’s supposed to be hard.”
Erin: He lets me climb on board and I have nowhere to hide.
UPSOUND – James Ketchell (01:05:41:10 – 01:05:48:41)
“Nothing worth having happens without effort and sacrifice.”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): British adventurer James Ketchell sails into Cape Town after months at sea — but this time, it’s not just about breaking records. He’s helping the South African Weather Service drop high-tech se
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An adventurer’s journey meets local science — James Ketchell’s Cape Town landing links exploration with the South African Weather Service’s work to better understand our oceans. Overview: British adventurer James Ketchell set sail from Gosport, England, on a nine-month, 30 000-nautical-mile journey around the world. His goal is to become the first person in history to circle the globe by air, land, and sea. Along the way, he connects with classrooms across the world — sharing lessons from the ocean and stories of endurance and discovery. Why Cape Town & South Africa Matter: Cape Town is one of the key stops on James’s global route. After months alone at sea, he’ll finally reunite with his family for a few days before continuing his voyage. While here, he’ll also work with the South African Weather Service to drop Argo floats — ocean sensors that gather important information about sea temperatures and currents. This data helps improve weather forecasts and climate research. What We’ll Cover: • The journey: James’s world challenge and what drives him to keep going. • The South African link: Cape Town as a crucial stop where science meets adventure. • The Argo floats: How they work and how they help local weather scientists. • The human story: Life alone on the ocean, and the emotional moment of seeing his family again. • The presenter’s experience: Our presenter will join James on the boat to get a real sense of what it takes to sail one of these yachts — from handling the ropes to facing the wind and waves. • Visuals: The Cape Town coastline, James’s arrival, his family reunion, the Argo floats, and sailing scenes with the presenter.
metadata.Summary: British adventurer James Ketchell arrives in Cape Town after months at sea on his solo circumnavigation. As part of his mission, he’s partnering with the South African Weather Service to deploy Argo floats — ocean sensors that collect vital climate and marine data. It’s a story that brings together human endurance, ocean science, and South Africa’s role in global research.
metadata.Further information: After months alone at sea, British adventurer James Ketchell is finally making landfall in Cape Town — greeted by his family for the first time in weeks. It’s an emotional reunion marking a rare pause in his nine-month, 30 000-nautical-mile solo voyage around the world. James is no stranger to pushing limits. He’s rowed across the Atlantic, climbed Mount Everest, and flown a gyrocopter around the globe. Now, his latest challenge brings him to South Africa — not only to continue his record-breaking journey, but also to work with the South African Weather Service. Together, they’ll deploy Argo floats, ocean instruments that drift beneath the waves to collect vital data about our climate and weather. Through this story, Carte Blanche goes beyond the adventure — exploring the man behind the mission, his long days alone on the ocean, and the brief, heartfelt moments that make the journey worthwhile.
